evidence.observation: Reads entire token row without any transaction or lock. Two concurrent requests can both read the same token row and both see revoked_at=NULL.
Standalone UPDATE, not wrapped in a transaction. There is no atomic check-and-set; the row can be read by another connection after the SELECT but before this UPDATE.
Two separate UPDATEs to revoke a family. Newly inserted token from the concurrent winner request is revoked by the second UPDATE because its revoked_at IS NULL.
Separate SELECT to check family revocation. Not part of the same transaction as the token lookup. In the concurrent flow the family is not yet revoked at the time request-2 performs this check.
No database-level constraint prevents duplicate rotation. The schema allows the race window to manifest.

hypotheses.statement: The entire rotate() sequence — findByHash, check revoked_at, revoke, insert — is not wrapped in a database transaction. Two concurrent requests both read the same unrevoked token row. Request-1 revokes the token and inserts a new one. Request-2 then finds row.revoked_at != null (stale from the initial read, confirmed on re-check), calls revokeFamily() which revokes request-1's newly-inserted token too, throws TokenReuseDetected, and the controller returns 401 + clearCookie → silent logout.
hypotheses.experiment: Execute rotate() twice concurrently with the same token. After both settle, query isFamilyRevoked for the family. If true, HR1 is confirmed — the family was erroneously revoked by a legitimate concurrent request.

hypotheses.statement: The second UPDATE in revokeFamily() (line 44-45) sweeps all revoked_at IS NULL tokens in the family, which catches the brand-new token inserted by the winning request just moments before, leaving the user with no valid refresh token.
hypotheses.experiment: After two concurrent refresh calls complete (one 200, one 401), count refresh_tokens rows WHERE family_id=X AND revoked_at IS NULL. If the count is 0, the new token was also swept — HR2 confirmed.
